sections.h2: Where to pay your Philadelphia property tax
sections.html:
Billing and collection of the Real Estate Tax belong to the Department of Revenue, and the Office of Property Assessment supplies the value the bill rests on. You pay once a year. One March 31 due date covers both the City and the School District.

  • Online: the Philadelphia Tax Center, using the property address or the OPA account number. An eCheck carries no processing charge, while debit and credit cards do.
  • By phone: (833) 913-0795.
  • By mail: check or money order payable to the City of Philadelphia, sent with the OPA account number to Department of Revenue, PO Box 8409, Philadelphia, PA 19101-8409.
  • In person: the Municipal Services Building at 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd. takes cash. Satellite offices at 7522 Castor Ave. and 2761 N. 22nd St. take no cash. Offices open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The rate for tax year 2025 is 1.3998 percent of assessed value.

sections.h2: What happens when a bill goes unpaid?
sections.html:
The account moves through a fixed ladder. Charges begin the day after the March 31 deadline and grow until the City treats the balance as delinquent and can move toward foreclosure.

  • From April 1: additions of 1.5 percent a month, running to January 1.
  • January 1: a further addition of up to 15 percent, a lien in the amount of the whole delinquency, and the account is registered delinquent.
  • February 1: penalties, attorney's fees and other costs are layered on.
  • Any time after that: legal action, which can end in a sheriff sale of the house at public auction.

The Department sends a Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure to accounts with a balance and no payment agreement. A current-year bill left unpaid through the end of the year lets the City start foreclosure, and debt from earlier years can be pursued at any time. The notice also points owners to free housing counseling and legal help through the City's housing agencies.

The Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, or OOPA, lets a homeowner who lives in the house repay old tax in monthly amounts tied to income. An owner whose name is not on the deed can qualify if a legal interest in the home can be shown, and no down payment is needed. Some low-income and senior households pay $0 a month.

Tiers 4 and 5 fold new year taxes into the agreement. Everyone else must pay each new March 31 bill in full on top of the monthly plan amount. Applicants show two forms of proof of residence, one a government photo ID, and income records such as tax returns, pay stubs or benefit letters. In tier 3, half the accrued interest is waived. A review of actual expenses is available when the tiered amount is unaffordable.

sections.h2: Other City charges that can become liens
sections.html:
Property tax is not the only debt that can attach to the parcel. The City can also file liens for several other charges:

  • Water and sewer charges, with questions going to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.
  • Commercial trash fees, previously called refuse fees.
  • Department of Licenses and Inspections abatement invoices.
  • Nuisance and demolition fees and fines.

Water liens can be searched at water-lien.phila.gov, which reports up to 15 years of recorded liens. A search there does not replace a title search, and it may omit court costs. If it shows a lien, a payoff request form goes to the Water Department by email.

The City runs several programs that cut a bill or spread it out, and the Tax Center has a combined application that checks eligibility for five of them at once. Owners already enrolled generally do not reapply unless the property changes hands.

  • The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable assessment of an owner-occupied home in 2027, and most owners save about $1,399.
  • The Real Estate Tax installment plan lets seniors and income-qualified owners pay the year in monthly installments instead of one lump sum.
  • The senior and low-income freezes hold the tax at its current level even if rates or values climb.
  • The Longtime Owner Occupants Program caps the taxable value for owners of ten or more years whose assessment jumped 50 percent in a year or 75 percent over five.
  • A credit applies to the City portion for reserve and National Guard members called to active duty.

Pennsylvania's own Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and adults with disabilities does not require a City tax receipt.

sections.h2: Selling a Philadelphia house when tax is due
sections.html:
Tax debt does not block a sale. The closing figure simply has to cover what the City is owed.

  1. Look up the balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center by address or OPA number.
  2. Search water-lien.phila.gov and send a water payoff form at least 30 days before settlement.
  3. Ask a housing counselor about an OOPA first if you want to stay in the home.
  4. Order a title search to catch trash fee, abatement and other liens.
  5. Budget for the 4.578 percent realty transfer tax and the deed recording fee.

A seller on a short clock can ask for a cash offer, and the title company settles the City's claim at the table. That route also skips repairs, listing prep and showings, which matters when a delinquent account is already moving toward the January 1 lien.

Philadelphia has a July 2025 population estimate of 1,574,281. A typical owned home is valued at $243,100, and 51.8 percent of households own, so renters make up nearly half. Median gross rent is $1,397 a month and median household income is $61,953. Neighborhood prices vary widely, so a countywide figure is only a rough guide for any one house.

sections.h2: What to have ready before a tax-related sale
sections.html:
Documents save time at the closing table. Gather the OPA account number, the latest tax bill and any Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure letter, and keep a copy of any signed payment agreement. Bring the water payoff response if a lien turned up. If you live in the house, tell the title company about your Homestead Exemption and any freeze, because the balance on file can differ from what you expect. If an agreement is active, ask the Department of Revenue how it is treated when the house sells, so the figure at settlement is not a surprise.

Keep paying the current bill while the sale is pending. Additions of 1.5 percent a month do not pause because a contract is signed, and a lien filed on January 1 would have to be paid from the proceeds.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Philadelphia property tax balance?
faqs.a: The Department of Revenue. You can check a balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center or call (833) 913-0795. Water charges go to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.

faqs.q: What if I cannot pay in full?
faqs.a: Apply for a payment agreement. An owner who lives in the house can ask for an OOPA, and owners who do not live there can request a standard agreement. Income-based programs can lower or pause payments.

faqs.q: Can Philadelphia take my house for unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, after the account becomes delinquent and a lien is filed. The City can then seek a court order to sell the house at a sheriff sale. A signed payment agreement or full payment stops the process.
They start April 1. Additions of 1.5 percent a month accrue from that date until January 1, when the larger delinquency charges apply.

faqs.q: Does the buyer or seller pay the tax at closing?
faqs.a: The seller covers what is owed through closing, taken from the seller's side of the settlement statement. The 4.578 percent transfer tax is normally split, though the City may collect it from either party.
